title: Tai chi
hookLine: in a trial, tai chi improved balance and reduced falls more than stretching (Li et al.)

cards: Early morning in a city park, a group of people move together as if underwater. Arms float up. Weight shifts from one foot to the other, so slowly it's hard to see where one movement ends and the next begins.
Nobody is sweating. Nobody is hurrying. A jogger goes past them twice.
It looks almost too gentle to do anything at all. A research team put that gentleness to the test, against two other kinds of exercise, with people whose balance was at real risk.

teach.b: First, what tai chi is: a Chinese practice of slow, flowing movement. Tradition links it to the martial arts and to Taoist ideas about softness and balance.

The name, taiji in Chinese, is usually translated the supreme ultimate. Second, the trial. A team led by Fuzhong Li worked with people living with Parkinson's disease, whose steadiness on their feet was a daily worry.
Over several months, they compared tai chi with strength training and with stretching. Third, the result.
The tai chi group improved more in balance than the other groups, and had fewer falls than the stretching group. Gentle turned out to be strong. Fourth, why slow might work, and an old echo.
Tai chi keeps shifting the weight from one leg to the other under control, so it's balance practice in disguise, and going slowly makes a person pay attention to the feet, the knees, the ground.
Earlier this year, reading the Tao Te Ching chapter by chapter, this path met its love of the soft: water that wears down what is hard, the young plant that is supple while it lives.

teach.h: THE SOFT, IN THE HIPS AND ANKLES.
teach.b: Tai chi puts that old idea into the hips and ankles.

teach.h: GENTLE TURNED OUT TO BE STRONG.
teach.b: The lab didn't test the Tao Te Ching. It tested slow movement, and slow movement held up.

how: People practice tai chi alone or in groups, often outdoors in parks, moving slowly through a set sequence of forms; some community and hospital programs teach it for balance.

games.q: you're designing a balance program for people living with Parkinson's disease. you can choose tai chi, strength training, or stretching. in Li's trial, which did best for balance?
games.why: tai chi improved balance more than both, and its group had fewer falls than the stretching group.

practice: If you can stand safely, stand with your feet about hip-width apart near something to hold; if not, stay seated.

Let your knees soften and shift your weight toward the right foot as slowly as you can, then back through the center and on to the left, arms floating a little if they want to. After a few shifts, sit, and let the body be still.
